item.title: Report: 49ers WR De'Zhaun Stribling to miss at least a month with an ankle injury
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The 49ers lost wide receiver De'Zhaun Stribling to an ankle injury on their way to a win over the Rams in Melbourne, Australia on Thursday and it will reportedly be a bit of time before the rookie is able to return to action.
item.content:encoded:
The 49ers lost wide receiver De'Zhaun Stribling to an ankle injury on their way to a win over the Rams in Melbourne, Australia on Thursday and it will reportedly be a bit of time before the rookie is able to return to action.

Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that Stribling is expected to be out for at least a month. Stribling is reportedly dealing with a deltoid sprain and is still consulting doctors about his options, but is not currently expected to need surgery.

The time frame makes Stribling a candidate for injured reserve.

Stribling was the first pick of the second round in this year's draft. He started against the Rams and played 21 snaps before leaving the game with his injury.

Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, and Demarcus Robinson are the top three wideouts for the Niners with Stribling out of action. All three of them caught touchdowns from Brock Purdy in Thursday's win.

item.title: Steelers, Joey Porter Jr. reach the moment of truth
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Steelers' outdated approach to contract negotiations is not aging well.
item.content:encoded:
The Steelers' outdated approach to contract negotiations is not aging well.

With the Steelers and cornerback Joey Porter Jr. in a financial standoff and the Steelers clinging to their policy of not doing new deals after the regular season begins, no deal will be done until after the season — unless the dam suddenly breaks this morning.

So will Porter play? Despite the ESPN report that it's "unlikely" Porter will suit up against the Falcons at 1:00 p.m. ET, some within the organization still believe he'll blink. Regardless of a contract that pays less than $4 million in 2026, Porter is in a contract year. His best play could be to play and to play well, setting the stage for a shot at the open market in 2027 or, worst-case scenario, the franchise tag. (The fact that the tag at the cornerback position lags behind the top pay at the position makes that outcome even less appealing.)

The alternative is to sit, citing a back problem. It's what Cowboys linebacker Micah Parsons likely planned to do in 2025, absent a new contract. Once the Cowboys realized he was committed to not playing, they traded him.

The latest ESPN report explains that the Steelers are open to listening to offers for Porter. Which is a delicate way of acknowledging that, as we've heard multiple times, no one has called.

This isn't some sudden realization that Porter could be available. He conducted a hold-in throughout training camp and the preseason. If anyone was interested in trading for Porter, they would have called by now.

The problem is that the new team would have to give the Steelers what they want for Porter, and to pay him what he's seeking. The absence of offers to date says plenty about the willingness of other teams to do that.

Which brings us back to Porter's primary options: Play for $3.924 million and hope to unlock a much better deal in 2027, or launch a Le'Veon Bell-style strategy (but with pay) — sitting out some if not most if not all games and becoming a free agent next year. (Or getting tagged.)

It's a tough spot for Porter. But there's one way to look at the glass as half-full. He was the 32nd pick in the 2023 draft, but he wasn't a first-rounder. He's not subject to the fifth-year option; for Year 5, he gets (at worst) franchise-tag money. That puts him ahead of where he would have been, if the Dolphins hadn't lost their 2023 first-round pick and if Porter had been the 32nd name off the board.

Regardless, Porter has to decide whether to take a stand by sitting out, or to grab his helmet and play. It's a decision that only Porter can make, and he needs to make it within the next couple of hours.

item.title: Jim Harbaugh tries to extend Week 1 record to 7-0
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: When it comes to the first game of football season, Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh does indeed attack the day with an enthusiasm unknown to mankind.
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to the first game of football season, Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh does indeed attack the day with an enthusiasm unknown to mankind.

Except for someone named "Potsy."

Harbaugh has a 6-0 record in Week 1, from his four seasons in San Francisco and two in L.A. With a win on Sunday against the Cardinals, he'll be 7-0 in Week 1.

And that will put him one more Week 1 win away from tying the all-time record. Via NBC Sports research, George "Potsy" Clark had a record of 8-0-2 in Week 1, from 1931 to 1940.

Clark's run started with the Portsmouth Spartans, who became the Detroit Lions. In 1937 and 1938, he coached the Brooklyn Dodgers. In 1940, his last year as an NFL head coach, Clark returned to the Lions.

It would be a surprise if the Chargers don't win today. They host the Cardinals (who have lost nine straight Week 1 games), and the home team is a 9.5-point favorite.

item.title: Justin Herbert needs 180 passing yards to be fourth-fastest to 25,000
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The quarterback whom Jim Harbaugh believes will be remembered as the greatest of all time has a chance to join the all-time greats on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The quarterback whom Jim Harbaugh believes will be remembered as the greatest of all time has a chance to join the all-time greats on Sunday.

With 180 passing yards, Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert will reach 25,000 yards for his career. It would make him the fourth-fastest quarterback in NFL history to get there, via NBC Sports research.

Herbert, if he does it, will have done it in 96 games. Patrick Mahomes got there in 83. Matthew Stafford crossed the 25K boundary in 90 games. And Dan Marino did it in 92.

It'll take much more than statistical achievements to earn "GOAT" status for Herbert. His first career playoff win, for example, would be a useful starting point.

Before that can happen, the Chargers have to qualify for the playoffs again. In a very competitive division and a conference featuring multiple wild-card contenders, it won't be easy. Between the Bills, Patriots, Bengals, Ravens, Steelers, Texans, Jaguars, Broncos, Chiefs, and Chargers, at least three will have their seasons end in Week 18.

item.title: Report: Lamar Jackson, Ravens have not had substantive contract talks
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson will play his first game under offensive coordinator Declan Doyle on Sunday and he's set to do so without a contract extension.
item.content:encoded:
Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson will play his first game under offensive coordinator Declan Doyle on Sunday and he's set to do so without a contract extension.

Jackson has a cap hit of more than $84 million for the 2027 season, which is the final year of his current deal. The Ravens have expressed desire to get a new deal done, but nothing has come together and Adam Schefter of ESPN reports that no substantive conversations have taken place about an agreement.

As a result, Jackson, who does not employ an agent, is expected to start the season under his current pact and will likely end it with the same deal as he prefers not to discuss contract matters during the season.

Ravens General Manager Eric DeCosta recently expressed optimism about reaching agreement on an extension before March 2027 and Sunday's report suggests that any deal will wait until much closer to that time.

item.title: Alvin Kamara is not expected to play on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Saints are set to open the 2026 season without running back Alvin Kamara.
item.content:encoded:
The Saints are set to open the 2026 season without running back Alvin Kamara.

Kamara suffered a sprained MCL last month and returned to practice this week. He was a limited participant for two days before fully participating in Friday's practice, but was listed as questionable on the team's final injury report.

Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that Kamara is not expected to play against the Lions as he continues to recover.

Free agent acquisition Travis Etienne will be the top back for New Orleans. Kendre Miller is the other running back on the 53-man roster and the Saints elevated CJ Donaldson from their practice squad for Sunday's game.

item.title: Report: Joey Porter Jr. is unlikely to play today, trade is possible
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Porter, who is listed as questionable with a back injury, looks like he won't go today against the Falcons.
item.content:encoded:
Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is unlikely to play today against the Falcons.

Porter, who is listed as questionable with a back injury, is unlikely to go, according to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport.

The same report says Porter could be traded, as he and the Steelers have still not come to terms on the new contract Porter is seeking. The Steelers have said they won't negotiate with Porter during the season.

Porter said during the week that if he didn't play, it would be because of both his back and because he still has some conditioning work he needs to do after sitting out training camp. He has not said that he will sit out games in protest of his contract status, although that's certainly an inference some will take if he doesn't play today.

Porter is heading into the final season of the four-year contract he signed as the Steelers' second-round draft pick in 2023. He's slated to make $3.9 million this year, and any team trading for him would need to be prepared to pay him a whole lot more than that.

item.title: Ryan Day: Ohio State considered letting Texas score, but decided we'd play defense
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: With 1:23 remaining in the fourth quarter on Saturday night, Ohio State led 23-17, but Texas had first-and-goal at the 1-yard line.
item.content:encoded:
With 1:23 remaining in the fourth quarter on Saturday night, Ohio State led 23-17, but Texas had first-and-goal at the 1-yard line. What Ohio State coach Ryan Day did from there will be one of the most-scrutinized decisions of this college football season.

Day could have called Ohio State's final timeout as soon as Texas got to first-and-goal, and then allowed Texas to score. That would have given Ohio State the ball back, down 24-23, with well over a minute remaining to mount a game-winning drive.

Instead, Ohio State stopped Texas on first and second down before Texas scored the game-winning touchdown on third down, with just 25 seconds left. Ohio State's desperation final drive lasted just two plays.

Day said after the game that letting Texas score was a consideration but he and his team ultimately thought they could play for a goal-line stand.

"I considered it, but I felt like at that point we were gonna go play defense and see if we could get off the field, but it didn't work out," Day said.

Day said he ultimately decided to have faith in his defense.

"We did, we talked about it, and decided that we were gonna play defense," Day said. "When we got that stop right there we said, alright, we're going to take our chances, put the ball down for one yard and see if we can stop them."

Ohio State couldn't stop them, and by the time Ohio State got the ball back, the Buckeyes were almost out of time — even though Ohio State also benefited from Texas snapping the ball too fast before scoring, when the Longhorns could have run even more time off the clock. Day decided to give his defense a chance to win the game, and that cost his offense the time to win the game.

item.title: Dante Moore struggles as Oregon loses to 24-point underdog Oklahoma State
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Oregon quarterback Dante Moore is a potential first overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft, but today he had a rough outing.
item.content:encoded:
Oregon quarterback Dante Moore is a potential first overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft, but today he had a rough outing.

Moore and Oregon lost 39-31 to 24-point underdog Oklahoma State today, with Moore completing less than 50 percent of his passes: Moore finished 14-of-29 for 191 yards, with two touchdowns and no interceptions.

How big a surprise is that? Oregon entered today ranked No. 6 in the country. Oklahoma State entered today on a 12-game losing streak, the longest in the country. Never before in college football history had a team on a losing streak of more than 10 games beaten a Top 10 opponent. Last year Oregon beat Oklahoma State 69-3.

Moore had moments when he showed off his elite arm talent, including touchdown passes of 38 and 36 yards. But he also struggled with his accuracy and had a hard time dealing with Oklahoma State's pass rush.

One bad game doesn't mean Moore won't be a top pick, but for a much-hyped prospect, today was a major disappointment.

item.title: Arch Manning puts "nightmares" behind him as Texas beats Ohio State
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: "I couldn't lose to them again. I had nightmares about that game last year," Manning said.
item.content:encoded:
A year ago, Texas entered the college football season ranked No. 1 and quarterback Arch Manning was viewed as a strong candidate to win the Heisman Trophy and be the first overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft. A loss to Ohio State derailed that. So when Manning and his Longhorns fell behind Ohio State 23-3 on Saturday night, it felt like déjà vu.

This time, however, things were different: Manning and the Texas offense marched down the field on three fourth-quarter touchdown drives to beat Ohio State 24-23.

"I couldn't lose to them again. I had nightmares about that game last year. So, we're glad to win tonight," Manning said on the field immediately after the game.

By the postgame press conference, Manning had settled down a bit, but he told reporters it was the same emotion about desperately wanting to beat the Ohio State team that had given him nightmares.

“I did not want to come in here after a loss at home, to Ohio State again, and have y'all tell me we’re not good, all that stuff. I could not let that happen," Manning said. "So that was going through my mind, let's not let that happen. Had to get something going. I always knew we were going to be in it at the end, we just had to get something going, and whatever it takes at the end of the game. I'm so glad we won."

Manning made some excellent throws but also missed some open receivers. He finished completing 23 of 37 passes for 195 yards, with one touchdown and one interception.

"It wasn't very pretty, but we found a way to win. That's what good teams do," Manning said.

Manning is now the favorite to be the first overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft. He still has a lot of football to play before then, but he's now earned his biggest win as a college quarterback, and put his biggest nightmare behind him.

item.title: Kyler Murray will be the ninth Vikings' starting QB since 2023
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: On Sunday, Kyler Murray will make his first start for the Vikings.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, Kyler Murray will make his first start for the Vikings. And he'll be the ninth quarterback to start a game for the Vikings since 2023.

Via NBC Sports research, that's tied for the most in the NFL during that stretch, with (not surprisingly) the Browns. (Cleveland has had 42 starters since returning to the NFL in 1999; no other team has started more than 30 during that same period of time.)

In 2022, coach Kevin O'Connell's first year with the Vikings, Kirk Cousins started all 17 regular-season games. He started the first eight in 2023, before tearing an Achilles tendon at Green Bay.

Since then, it's been Jaren Hall (two games), Joshua Dobbs (four), Nick Mullens (four), Sam Darnold (all 17 in 2024), J.J. McCarthy (10), Carson Wentz (five), and Max Brosmer (two).

Given that Wentz and McCarthy are currently on the roster and Brosmer is on the practice squad, the Vikings likely won't start a tenth different quarterback in 2026.

In 2022 and 2024, when the same guy started every game, the Vikings made the playoffs. The hope will be that Murray manages to start all 17 in 2026 — and that the Vikings get back to the postseason.

item.title: To no surprise, the Texans and C.J. Stroud will kick the contract can to 2027
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Nothing says "football is back" like the issuance of Sunday Splash!
item.content:encoded:
Nothing says "football is back" like the issuance of Sunday Splash! reports on a Saturday.

Per ESPN, the Texans and quarterback C.J. Stroud won’t get a deal done before the start of the season. Which means they'll now wait until after the season ends to assess the situation.

The notion that there won't be an in-season deal was already known. G.M. Nick Caserio recently said so.

The idea that there won't be a deal before Week 1 wasn't etched in stone, but the handwriting was written on the wall in permanent marker.

Would the Texans sign Stroud to a deal based on his performances to date? Yes. Would Stroud accept it? No.

Houston's preferred range likely won't get any lower based on 2026. A strong year from Stroud could push it much higher.

Even after the coming season, there may be no reason for the Texans to rush it. Stroud remains under contract through 2027. They'd be negotiating against themselves, like the Dolphins did when they gave Tua Tagovailoa what turned out to be a disastrous the-market-is-the-market deal in 2024.

Actually, the Texans could let it ride for two more years, with the franchise tag in their back pockets in the event Stroud suddenly reaches a higher level of performance.

If he was already there, the Texans wouldn't hesitate to pay him. They did it after three seasons with cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. They did it after three seasons with linebacker Will Anderson.

They would have done it with Stroud, too. But only at the number that properly reflects his spot in a range that now extends from $20 million per year to $64 million annually.

The Texans remain committed to Stroud. They didn't bench him at halftime of a disastrous divisional-round game against the Patriots, even though they arguably should have. They want him to become a player who forces the Texans to pay him big money.

For now, Stroud has to go out and show that he deserves it.

item.title: Our opposition to the Protect College Sports Act prompted a phone call from Randy Levine
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Earlier today, we posted an item about ESPN's advocacy for the Protect College Sports Act.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier today, we posted an item about ESPN's advocacy for the Protect College Sports Act. The latest example of ESPN's effort to turn the bill into a law was a one-sided interview with Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the act's sponsors.

I said what I had to say. I heard from multiple members of the media, who agreed with the sentiments that were expressed.

But not everyone agreed. At 5:45 p.m. ET, I got a phone call from a number I didn't recognize.

It was Randy Levine, president of the New York Yankees and vice-chair (along with Ron DeSantis) of President Trump's Saving College Sports Roundtable.

Did I immediately know who Randy Levine was? No. Did that set the stage for a call that didn't go very well? Possibly.

He said he wanted to correct some of the statements made in our article about the Cruz interview, by ensuring that I have the facts. I told him that I always want to operate within the confines of any and all relevant facts.

Levine then explained that, in his view, collective bargaining is an impossibility for college sports. He pointed to the fact that most universities are public institutions, that the federal labor laws do not apply to public employment, and that it would require a change in the Federal Labor Relations Act, which dates back to the 1930s.

When I observed that the NCAA is instead trying to change federal antitrust laws that have been on the books even longer than that, Levine didn't seem to appreciate my point.

I wanted to explain to him that the prevalence of commentary regarding the possibility of collective bargaining from various corners of the college-sports ecosystems suggests that it's hardly a non-starter. Laws can be changed. Private entities can be created. Conferences, which aren't public entities, could be the conduit for an acceptable model that would give the NCAA and its members the antitrust exemption that flows from maintaining a multi-employer bargaining unit — which is how the NFL has managed to engineer a path around the antitrust laws.

Indeed, Pac-12 Commissioner Teresa Gould said in June 2026 testimony before the Senate Commerce Committee that it’s time for “honest conversations” about collective bargaining. Common sense suggests that, if collective bargaining is impossible, there are no conversations to be had.

My conversation with Levine didn't get to that point, however. After I allowed him to speak his mind on the collective bargaining issue, I began to respond, by pointing out the effort to change long-settled federal antitrust laws. He interrupted me. I asked him to let me finish my point. He then launched into the "do you want pro athletes going back to college?" talking point. I told him, bluntly but politely, that the "pro athletes" in question had signed tryout contracts and opted to try to make more money by returning to college football, after they were not offered NFL roster spots.

I also told Levine that the entire "pro athlete going back to college" argument is a fallacy, and that college athletes are already pro athletes.

And, at that point, he ended the call.

Before doing so, Levine pointed out he'd tell everyone that I don't know what I'm talking about, or words to that effect.

Good luck with that, Randy. Many people already think I don't know what I'm talking about. That has rarely stopped me from talking, however.

Bottom line? We've apparently struck a nerve. Really, why would Levine have taken the time to call me on a Saturday afternoon?

The Saving College Sports Roundtable is apparently concerned that this small corner of the Internet may have a little bit of influence when it comes to calling the Protect College Sports Act what it is, and when it comes to mustering real opposition to a flawed bill that will be bad for players.

The Jaguars and wide receiver Parker Washington are unlikely to reach a contract extension before the start of the season, Cameron Wolfe of NFL Media reports.

Washington is in the final year of his rookie deal, scheduled to make $3.722 million this season.

The 2023 sixth-round pick posted career highs last season with 58 catches for 847 yards and five touchdowns.

He also returned a pair of punts for touchdowns.

item.title: Patriots place WR A.J. Brown on IR, officially sign DT DaQuan Jones
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Patriots made official the signing of veteran defensive tackle DaQuan Jones.
item.content:encoded:
The Patriots made official the signing of veteran defensive tackle DaQuan Jones. To get him on the roster, the Patriots needed to open a spot.

New England did that by placing wide receiver A.J. Brown on injured reserve.

Brown, who has a high-ankle sprain, will not be eligible to return until missing at least four games. He will not play against the Steelers, Jaguars, Bills and Raiders.

item.title: NAACP takes issue with ESPN's handling of the Protect College Sports Act
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: On Saturday, ESPN gave Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) a platform to push for the passage of the Protect College Sports Act.
item.content:encoded:
On Saturday, ESPN gave Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) a platform to push for the passage of the Protect College Sports Act. There was no balance, no equal time.

And ESPN is receiving the criticism it deserves for its ongoing effort to support the bill.

The NAACP has responded. The organization, which seeks to "achieve equity, political rights, and social inclusion by advancing policies and practices that expand human and civil rights, eliminate discrimination, and accelerate the well-being, education, and economic security of Black people and all persons of color," has posted the following statement on Twitter: "Surprised [ESPN] so willing[ly] lent their platform to political performance today. But we’ll play. We’d love to have [NCAA president Derrick Johnson] join you in his home state of Miss. next week to express why the Protect College Sports Act is dangerous to Black Athletes and the Black community."

The proponents of the Protect College Sports Act don't want you to think of it that way. They want you to see unrestrained chaos in college sports — created by the reckoning for years of antitrust violations — and they believe the only answer is to give the NCAA and its members an antitrust exemption that will allow the earning power and mobility of players to be limited.

The broader point is that ESPN is clearly in the tank for the passage of the Protect College Sports Act. If it isn't, it will give Derrick Johnson a chance next weekend to state the case against it, when College GameDay goes to Oxford for LSU vs. Ole Miss.

item.title: Judge seals video in Josh Jacobs case
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The video of the altercation that resulted in Packers running back Josh Jacobs pleading no contest to multiple misdemeanor charges could complicate his football career, if/when it's ever released.
item.content:encoded:
The video of the altercation that resulted in Packers running back Josh Jacobs pleading no contest to multiple misdemeanor charges could complicate his football career, if/when it's ever released.

For now, it won't be.

Via James Stratton of WISN, Judge Marc Hammer has signed an order “temporarily” sealing the evidence in the case. Including the video.

The sealing of the evidence was requested not by the prosecution or by the victim but by Jacobs.

From the order: "The Court finds that public disclosure of the Discovery Material would threaten or substantially impair Defendant’s and [the victim's] privacy, dignity, personal security, emotional wellbeing, or ability to participate safely in the criminal-justice process. This protection is not to impede any legitimate law-enforcement function, criminal prosecution judicial proceeding, or disclosure otherwise required by law, but to prevent unnecessary public dissemination of information that identifies [the victim], reveals intimate or sensitive details of [the victim] or the Defendant, or creates a material risk of harm."

The order was granted "pending a further Motion to be filed by [the victim] and/or Defendant."

The situation creates a quandary for the NFL. Will the league tell Jacobs he can't play until he asks for the video to be released? Or will the league welcome the reality that the video won't be seen by the general public?

The situation conjures instant memories of the notorious Ray Rice video. The league didn't insist on seeing it. Then, TMZ obtained it. All hell broke loose for the NFL, with Rice's career ending and the Commissioner spending a week or so wondering whether he'd have to resign, after the Associated Press reported that the NFL had seen the video before it was published.

Video changes everything. Knowing what happened is one thing; seeing it is another.

Why else would Jacobs want it to be hidden from view? It will be interesting to see whether the league tries to force Jacobs to secure the video's release, or whether it shrugs at the fact that it's not available.

For now, Jacobs is on paid leave. He'll remain there until the NFL determines the discipline to be imposed under the Personal Conduct Policy. How can it properly determine the discipline without seeing the video?

item.title: Amon-Ra St. Brown needs only 33 catches for most ever through six NFL seasons
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Five years after entering the NFL as a fourth-round pick, Lions receiver Amon-Ra St.
item.content:encoded:
Five years after entering the NFL as a fourth-round pick, Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown won't need much time in his sixth season to make history. Again.

St. Brown already has the record for the most catches by any player through five seasons, with 547. It's an average of 109.4 per season. And his production through five years will make it easy to set the record for the most catches through six seasons.

Via NBC Sports research, St. Brown needs only 33 catches in 2026 to break the current record of 579, which was set last year by Vikings receiver Justin Jefferson.

St. Brown is a four-time Pro Bowler, a two-time first-team All-Pro, and a one-time second-team All-Pro. Coupled with Jameson Williams, the Lions have one of the top one-two punches at the receiver position. Throw in running back Jahmyr Gibbs, and it truly is amazing that the Lions not only missed the playoffs in 2025 but also finished last in the NFC North.

That should change in 2026, especially with the Lions getting the benefit of a fourth-place schedule. With the Bears drawing the Texans, Eagles, and Seahawks and the Packers getting the Jaguars, Cowboys, and Rams, the Lions will face the Titans, Giants, and Cardinals.

In a division that had first place and fourth place separated by only two games, those three games could be all the difference the Lions need.

item.title: ESPN continues its not-so-subtle advocacy for the Protect College Sports Act
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: I said it this week on PFT Live.
item.content:encoded:
I said it this week on PFT Live. And I'll say it again now.

Anyone who supports the Protect College Sports Act opposes player rights.

Those who are speaking out in support of the bill won't admit it. We'll do it for them. Under the guise of ending chaos tracing to decades of antitrust violations that denied the players the ability to earn anything for their skills, sacrifices, and fame, the proponents of the bill want to limit the amount of money that goes to players, diverting it to the programs.

That's the fundamental problem none of them will ever acknowledge. There are only so many dollars that can be siphoned from the piggybanks of the boosters. Every dollar that goes to an NIL fund is one less dollar that can go to the program. They want to reduce what can go to the players, maximizing what can go to the programs.

Unwilling to embrace a nationwide union that would allow the creation of a salary cap, transfer limits, and other rules aimed at creating order, the powers-that-be crave an exemption from the laws that prevent the universities from coming together and crafting anticompetitive — and anticapitalist — restrictions on the players' earning power and freedom to transfer. And ESPN has been leading the conga line, with influential voices like Nick Saban and Pat McAfee openly pushing the Protect College Sports Act.

On Saturday, ESPN gave Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the sponsors of the bill, an extended interview during College GameDay to press the case for passage of the proposed law. Cruz, not surprisingly, opened by pointing to the LSU and Brendan Sorsby situations as evidence of the current chaos. The loud reaction to those specific situations was always about mustering political momentum to get the bill passed.

Cruz also claimed that there currently is a "[s]piral of costs that is bankrupting almost every college program in the country. . . . They’re losing tens of millions of dollars." That contention, to use a technical term, is horseshit.

There was no opposing viewpoint offered in response, other than the organic and incessant booing of Cruz (which included a one point a "Ted you suck!" chant). No time was provided for those who have concerns about the bill.

At one point, host Rece Davis posed a perfunctory question to Cruz regarding the absence of limits on compensation and mobility for coaches and administrators. Cruz offered an evasive word salad in response, and he received no pushback.

Contrary to what ESPN is leading its viewers to believe, the bill has real opposition. On Monday, Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) will conduct a press conference at noon ET with "college athletes, professional athlete unions, families and advocates" to address the problems with the bill.

From the email announcing the event, "participants will detail how the bill denies college athletes the rights and protections they are owed as workers and cuts off any path these athletes have to advocate for themselves — all so the NCAA, college athletic conferences and schools can consolidate money and power over athletes’ lives."

Why wasn't Murphy given equal time on College GameDay? Cruz and Murphy could have debated the merits and problems with the bill. While there are no safe bets in this age of bet! bet! bet!, it would be safe to wager the farm on ESPN not preempting McAfee's show and taking Murphy's press conference live as it happens on Monday.
